title: Century City
name: Century City
metaTitle: Century City in Los Angeles, CA
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for Century City office towers, condominium-interest floors, and Westfield-anchored retail in this concentrated Los Angeles submarket.

sections.html: Century City is a single master-planned business district built on the former Twentieth Century Fox backlot, and nearly all of its commercial inventory sits in a small cluster of high-rise office towers and one large retail center. An exchange buyer targeting Century City is choosing a concentrated, high-barrier office and retail market rather than a broad submarket with dozens of comparable buildings.

sections.heading: A Backlot Built Into Office Towers
sections.html:
Fox Plaza and Constellation Place anchor a district that grew directly out of studio land, and the tenant base leans heavily toward entertainment law, talent representation, and financial services firms that value proximity to the studios and agencies clustered nearby. That tenant concentration means lease terms and credit profiles in Century City often look different from a more diversified downtown or Westside office building, with longer average lease terms among professional-services anchor tenants.

A replacement buyer reviewing a Century City tenant roster should ask how much of the building's income depends on a small number of large law-firm or agency floors rather than a broad base of smaller tenants, since a single anchor departure can move occupancy meaningfully in a tower with only a handful of major leases. That concentration cuts both ways: a strong, long-tenured anchor tenant can make the income stream unusually stable, while a lease expiring mid-hold period can create a re-leasing gap that takes longer to fill than in a more diversified building.

sections.heading: Condo Ownership and a Thin Bench of Sellers
sections.html:
Some Century City office space trades as individually owned commercial condominiums rather than whole-building assets, which changes how a replacement property search runs. A buyer used to whole-building net lease deals should confirm whether a Century City opportunity is a full-building acquisition or a partial-floor condominium interest, since financing, governance, and exit liquidity differ substantially between the two.

Governing documents on a condominium-interest floor also dictate how much control an owner actually has over leasing, signage, and building services, and those documents should be reviewed alongside the rent roll rather than treated as a closing-day formality. A qualified intermediary coordinating this kind of purchase should confirm the escrow and title team has handled a commercial condominium interest before, since the closing mechanics differ from a standard whole-building transfer in ways that can slow down the back half of an exchange timeline if discovered late.

sections.heading: What Trades in This District
sections.html:
The realistic Century City identification list is narrow but well defined:

  • Class A high-rise office floors and full-floor condominium interests
  • ground-floor and second-level retail space in or adjacent to Westfield Century City
  • medical and professional office suites serving the surrounding Westside population
  • structured parking assets tied to office and retail buildings

sections.heading: The District's Single Retail Draw
sections.html: Westfield Century City functions as the district's only large retail draw, and its recent repositioning toward luxury and experiential tenants has pulled in higher-end retailers than the district saw a decade ago. A retail replacement property here is really a bet on that single center's continued draw, since there is little competing retail inventory inside Century City itself, and comparable sales data has to be pulled from neighboring Westside centers rather than from within the district.

sections.heading: Why Century City Rarely Stands Alone on a List
sections.html:
Because the total inventory of investable Century City buildings is small, most exchange buyers who identify a Century City property pair it with a West Los Angeles or Beverly Hills alternative to keep a three-property list workable. Lenders and appraisers familiar with condo-interest office financing move faster here than generalist commercial lenders, and confirming that familiarity early avoids a financing delay inside the 180-day exchange period.

Comparable sales data inside Century City itself is thin simply because so few buildings trade in any given year, so appraisers frequently pull secondary comparables from West Los Angeles and Beverly Hills office towers to round out a valuation. A buyer should expect that blended comparable set and ask an appraiser directly how much weight was given to true Century City sales versus nearby Westside comparables, since the gap between the two markets has widened at times over the past several years.

faqs.q: Is Century City office space typically owned as whole buildings or as condominium interests?
faqs.a: Both structures exist in the district, and a buyer should confirm which one applies to a specific opportunity early, since condominium interests carry different financing and governance requirements than a whole-building acquisition.

faqs.q: What kind of tenants occupy Century City office towers?
faqs.a: Entertainment law, talent representation, and financial services firms make up a large share of the tenant base, drawn by proximity to nearby studios and agencies, and that concentration should factor into any credit analysis of an in-place rent roll.

faqs.q: Is there meaningful industrial or multifamily inventory in Century City?
faqs.a: No. The district is almost entirely office, retail, and structured parking, so investors looking for industrial or multifamily replacement property should expect to look at neighboring West Los Angeles or Beverly Hills instead.

faqs.q: How much does Westfield Century City matter to a retail replacement decision here?
faqs.a: It matters significantly, since the mall is the district's only large retail draw and most nearby retail space depends on the foot traffic it generates rather than standing on its own.

faqs.q: Why do Century City identifications often pair with a second submarket?
faqs.a: The district's total building count is small, so pairing a Century City identification with a West Los Angeles or Beverly Hills alternative keeps a three-property list from depending entirely on a single tight, low-inventory market.
